title: Remove Max Number of Edges to Keep Graph Fully Traversable
description: Brute force to optimized: trying every edge subset directly versus two Union-Find structures with shared edges processed first.

sections.title: Remove Max Number of Edges to Keep Graph Fully Traversable

content.title: Remove Max Number of Edges to Keep Graph Fully Traversable

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Alice and Bob need to fully traverse an undirected graph of n nodes independently. Each edge is type 1 (Alice only), type 2 (Bob only), or type 3 (both). Return the maximum number of edges that can be removed while both Alice and Bob can still fully traverse the entire graph (reach every node from any other), or -1 if not possible even with all edges present.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","n, edges typed 1/2/3"],["Output","Maximum removable edges, or -1"],["Key Insight","Greedily use type-3 edges FIRST (they help both people simultaneously), then only add type-1/type-2 edges where a person still needs additional connectivity"],["Constraints","Up to 10^5 edges"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Keep the minimum edges needed for TWO separate people to each fully traverse a graph\"","Union-Find, with a greedy priority: shared (type-3) edges are strictly more valuable than single-use edges, so process them first"]]}

blocks.text: Maintain TWO separate Union-Find structures, one for Alice's reachability and one for Bob's. Since a type-3 edge helps BOTH people simultaneously, it should always be used FIRST whenever it usefully connects two previously separate components in either person's structure (or both). Only AFTER exhausting the benefit of all type-3 edges should type-1 edges be added (only for Alice, only where still needed) and type-2 edges (only for Bob, only where still needed). The total number of edges actually needed is the "used" count; the answer is the total edge count minus this used count, or -1 if either person's structure never becomes fully connected.

blocks.title: Analogy: Building Shared and Private Roads to Connect Two Different Delivery Networks Cheaply
blocks.text: Picture building roads to connect all cities for two separate delivery companies, where some roads can be used by BOTH companies, and some are restricted to just one. Building the shared roads first maximizes their value (helping both companies at once), only adding a company-specific road afterward if that company still has cities it cannot otherwise reach.

blocks.caption: Use type-3 edges first (helping both), then add type-1/type-2 edges only where still needed

blocks.text: Result: 1 (the redundant type-3 edge [1,3] can be removed, since 1 and 3 are already connected via 2).

Result: -1 (Bob has no way to connect node 1, since the only edges touching it are type-3 to node 2 and type-1, neither of which helps Bob reach node 1 from node 4... actually here Bob cannot fully traverse, hence impossible).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A type-3 edge is strictly more valuable than a type-1 or type-2 edge, since it can help connect components for BOTH Alice and Bob simultaneously with just one edge.

Observation 2: Processing ALL type-3 edges first, using each one in BOTH Alice's and Bob's Union-Find structures (counting it as "used" if it usefully merges components in EITHER structure), maximizes the shared benefit before considering any single-purpose edges.

Observation 3: After processing every type-3 edge, process type-1 edges (Alice only) and type-2 edges (Bob only), adding each only if it still USEFULLY connects two currently separate components in its respective structure.

Observation 4: After processing everything, if either Alice's or Bob's structure has more than one remaining component (not fully connected), return -1; otherwise, the answer is the total edge count minus however many edges were actually "used" (needed) across both structures.
This leads to two Union-Find structures, processing type-3 edges first (greedily, for maximum shared benefit), then type-1/type-2 edges only where still needed.
Conceptually, try every possible subset of edges to KEEP, checking whether both Alice's and Bob's reachability requirements are satisfied for each subset, keeping the smallest valid subset.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every subset directly implements the definition of "find the minimum edges needed" literally.
This costs O(2 raised to the number of edges), utterly infeasible for up to 10^5 edges; a greedy Union-Find approach, prioritizing shared edges, finds the optimal answer directly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 raised to edges) to enumerate all subsets.
Space: O(n) per subset check.
Limitation: the greedy strategy of using shared (type-3) edges first, only supplementing with single-purpose edges where still needed, is provably optimal and runs in near-linear time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain two separate Union-Find structures, aliceDSU and bobDSU. First, process every type-3 edge: union it in BOTH structures, and count it as "used" if it usefully merged components in EITHER structure. Then, process every type-1 edge, unioning it in aliceDSU only, counting it as used if it merged components; similarly process every type-2 edge in bobDSU only. After all processing, check if BOTH aliceDSU and bobDSU are fully connected (every node in one single component); if not, return -1. Otherwise, return the total edge count minus the total "used" count.
Use two Union-Find structures, processing shared type-3 edges first, then type-1/type-2 edges only where still needed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge processed","Effect"],"rows":[["[3,1,2]","unites 1,2 in BOTH structures, used=1"],["[3,2,3]","unites {1,2},3 in BOTH structures, used=2"],["[3,1,3]","already connected in both, NOT used (redundant)"],["[1,2,4]","unites 4 in aliceDSU, used=3"],["[2,3,4]","unites 4 in bobDSU, used=4"],["Final","both fully connected; answer = 5 edges total - 4 used = 1"]]}

blocks.text: Processing type-3 edges first is optimal because a shared edge can NEVER be worse than using two separate type-1 and type-2 edges to achieve the same two connections, so greedily using shared edges whenever they usefully merge components (in either structure) never wastes potential; only after exhausting this shared benefit are single-purpose edges added, and only where STILL strictly needed (a redundant edge, one connecting already-unified components, contributes nothing and is correctly left unused, becoming removable); the final connectivity check correctly detects whether the graph, even using every edge, can never satisfy both people's full traversal requirement.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(edges times inverse Ackermann function), effectively linear.
Space: O(n) for each Union-Find structure.

blocks.text: Remove Max Number of Edges to Keep Graph Fully Traversable is a strong example of a greedy Union-Find strategy: prioritize the most "valuable" (shared) resource first, only supplementing with single-purpose resources where strictly necessary.

items: Processing type-1 and type-2 edges BEFORE type-3 edges, potentially using a type-1 edge where a later type-3 edge would have made it redundant, missing an optimal removal.
Forgetting to check BOTH Alice's and Bob's full connectivity at the end, missing the -1 case where one person cannot fully traverse.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["No type-3 edges at all","Alice and Bob must each independently achieve full connectivity using only their own type-specific edges."],["A node with no edges reaching it at all","Neither Alice nor Bob can ever fully traverse, correctly returning -1."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "process shared edges first, since they are strictly more valuable than single-purpose edges" demonstrates the key greedy insight and why it is provably optimal.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "minimize edges needed for two separate parties to each achieve full connectivity", think: two Union-Find structures, greedily processing shared edges before single-purpose ones.

items: How would you extend this to THREE or more parties, some edges shared among various subsets of them?
Accounts Merge and Number of Provinces, other Union-Find applications, though without this problem's greedy "process shared resources first" twist.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force subset search costs O(2 raised to edges), utterly infeasible; the greedy two-Union-Find approach costs effectively linear time, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: two Union-Find structures, with a greedy priority: process shared resources before single-purpose ones.
Core Idea: type-3 edges help both people at once, so use them first; only add type-1/type-2 edges where still strictly needed afterward.
Time: O(2^edges) for the brute force, effectively linear for the greedy Union-Find approach.
Space: O(n) per subset for the brute force, O(n) for the greedy approach.
Most Important Observation: a shared edge is never worse than two separate single-purpose edges achieving the same connections.
Interview Difficulty: a hard, elegant greedy Union-Find problem.
One line memory trick: shared edges first, then fill gaps per person.
